title: Newsdesk story: three memorials
lede: A short three-story flight to official memorials at Hiroshima, Robben Island and the Normandy American Cemetery, cited from UNESCO, UNESCO, and the American Battle Monuments Commission. Pins are approximate or rounded from a listed UNESCO point.

cards.title: Hiroshima Peace Memorial
cards.body: The UNESCO World Heritage Centre page for the Hiroshima Peace Memorial (Genbaku Dome), list 775, says the memorial was the only structure left standing in the area where the first atomic bomb exploded on 6 August 1945, that it has been preserved in the same state as immediately after the bombing, and that it expresses the hope for world peace and the ultimate elimination of all nuclear weapons. Date of inscription is 1996. The brief synthesis identifies the ruin as the surviving remains of the Hiroshima Prefectural Industrial Promotional Hall, constructed in 1914, and gives the inscribed property as 0.40 hectares, with a 42.7-hectare buffer zone that includes the Peace Memorial Park.
cards.why: An official World Heritage memorial of a mapped historic event.

stories.title: Robben Island, a World Heritage prison site
stories.summary: UNESCO describes Robben Island as having been used between the 17th and 20th centuries as a prison, a hospital for socially unacceptable groups, and a military base. Its late-20th-century maximum security prison for political prisoners, it says, witnesses the triumph of democracy and freedom over oppression and racism.

stories.script: UNESCO describes Robben Island as a prison, hospital and military base between the 17th and 20th centuries, whose late-20th-century maximum security prison for political prisoners witnesses the triumph of democracy and freedom over oppression and racism. The pin is approximate.

captions.text: UNESCO: a prison site that witnesses democracy's triumph.

cards.title: Robben Island
cards.body: The UNESCO World Heritage Centre page for Robben Island (list 916) says the island was used at various times between the 17th and 20th centuries as a prison, a hospital for socially unacceptable groups and a military base, and that its buildings, particularly the late-20th-century maximum security prison for political prisoners, witness the triumph of democracy and freedom over oppression and racism. The brief synthesis also notes 17th-century quarries and a maximum security prison of the Apartheid period that began in the 1960s, and says this use came to an end in the 1990s when political prisoners received their freedom. The official 2001 UNESCO World Heritage List PDF records the inscription year as 1999 (id 916). The listed property area is 475 hectares.
cards.why: An official World Heritage account of a mapped site of imprisonment and political change.

stories.title: Normandy American Cemetery at Colleville-sur-Mer
stories.summary: The American Battle Monuments Commission says the cemetery at Colleville-sur-Mer stands on the site of the temporary American St. Laurent Cemetery, established by the U.S. First Army on 8 June 1944 as the first American cemetery on European soil in World War II. It was dedicated in 1956.

location.note: Approximate pin for the ABMC cemetery above the Normandy landing beaches. A surveyed gate coordinate is [UNKNOWN] in this card. Not a street address.

stories.script: The American Battle Monuments Commission says the Normandy American Cemetery at Colleville-sur-Mer stands on the site of the temporary St. Laurent Cemetery, established by the U.S. First Army on 8 June 1944. The cemetery was dedicated in 1956. The pin is approximate.

captions.text: On the first American cemetery site of 8 June 1944.

cards.title: Normandy American Cemetery
cards.body: The official American Battle Monuments Commission page lists the Normandy American Cemetery at Colleville-sur-Mer, France, as dedicated in 1956, covering 172.5 acres, with 9,389 burials and 1,557 missing in action. The overview says it stands on the site of the temporary American St. Laurent Cemetery, established by the U.S. First Army on 8 June 1944 as the first American cemetery on European soil in World War II, and that most of those buried lost their lives in the D-Day landings and ensuing operations. An official American Battle Monuments Commission booklet dates the dedication to 18 July 1956.
cards.why: An official U.S. overseas cemetery on the mapped D-Day shore.
